# Comparison with related tools

Quarto-Needs is new. This page exists so that someone evaluating it can
decide against it quickly and for the right reasons.

## How this page was verified {#verification}

Every claim about another tool was read from that project's own
documentation or source at the version named below, on **10 September
2026**. Nothing here is written from memory or inferred from a feature's
name. Where a claim could not be confirmed from a primary source it says
*not verified* rather than guessing — an empty cell is worth more than a
plausible one.

Versions verified against:

| Tool | Version | Released | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sphinx-Needs | 8.5.0 | 2026-09-03 | [PyPI](https://pypi.org/project/sphinx-needs/), [docs](https://sphinx-needs.readthedocs.io/en/latest/) |
| StrictDoc | 0.29.0 | 2026-08-30 | [PyPI](https://pypi.org/project/strictdoc/), [docs](https://strictdoc.readthedocs.io/en/stable/), [source at tag 0.29.0](https://github.com/strictdoc-project/strictdoc/tree/0.29.0) |
| Doorstop | 3.2 | 2026-07-10 | [PyPI](https://pypi.org/project/Doorstop/), [docs](https://doorstop.readthedocs.io/) |
| OpenFastTrace | 4.9.0 | 2026-08-07 | [GitHub release](https://github.com/itsallcode/openfasttrace/releases), [user guide](https://github.com/itsallcode/openfasttrace/blob/main/doc/user_guide/user_guide.md) |
| Quarto-Needs | 0.1.1 | 2026-09-09 | this repository |

Requirements tools move. Any row here is a statement about one version on
one date, and re-checking before relying on it is reasonable.

## Not compared: DOORS, Polarion, Codebeamer {#commercial}

These are a different category, not stronger competitors in the same one.
They are sold with support contracts, tool-qualification packages for
IEC 61508 / ISO 26262 / DO-178C, training, and per-seat licensing, and they
are typically chosen through procurement rather than by the engineers who
will use them. An organisation that needs a qualified tool with a vendor
liable for it is not choosing between DOORS and a single-maintainer
open-source project, and a row-by-row table pretending otherwise would
discredit the rest of this page. If tool qualification is a requirement,
none of the five tools compared below satisfies it.

## The comparison {#table}

Quarto-Needs entries carry their stability tier, taken from the
[stability registry](stability.qmd). Untagged means stable.

| | Quarto-Needs 0.1.1 | Sphinx-Needs 8.5.0 | StrictDoc 0.29.0 | Doorstop 3.2 | OpenFastTrace 4.9.0 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Authoring** | `.need` blocks inside Quarto `.qmd` prose | `need` directives in reStructuredText inside a Sphinx project[^sn-docs] | `.sdoc` files in its own grammar, also editable through a web GUI[^sd-map] | one YAML file per item, grouped into document directories[^ds-index] | tags in source-code and markup comments, plus specification items in Markdown/RST[^oft-formats] |
| **Where the semantics live** | Python core independent of the renderer; the Quarto extension is an adapter and the CLI runs without rendering | inside the Sphinx build — Sphinx-Needs is "an extension for the Python based Sphinx documentation framework"[^sn-docs] | standalone tool with its own exporters and web server[^sd-map] | standalone tool; publishing is a separate command[^ds-publish] | standalone Java tool, requires Java 17+[^oft-readme] |
| **Coverage gating** | percentage gates with thresholds, distinguishing a link existing (`-trace`) from the link meaning something (`-effective`, `-successful`) | boolean conditions via `needs_warnings`, failing the build with Sphinx `-W`; `needreport usage` reports counts, and no percentage threshold is documented[^sn-config][^sn-report] | *not verified* — a query engine and a project-statistics screen exist, both marked experimental by the project[^sd-features]; no coverage-threshold gate found | validation reports errors and warnings, including items with no links from a child document; no percentage threshold documented[^ds-validate] | distinguishes **shallow** from **deep** coverage and reports transitive defects, with a non-zero exit on defects[^oft-guide] |
| **Execution evidence** | `evidence check` / `evidence attest` (preview) validate a pytest artifact against the graph | via a separate extension, sphinx-test-reports 1.4.0, which imports XML test results as needs[^sn-testreports] | reads JUnit XML and Robot XML test reports and GCov coverage as part of tree discovery[^sd-junit] | *not verified* | tests cover requirements through the same tags as any other artifact type[^oft-guide] |
| **Change analysis** | baseline `diff` / `impact`; Git-range `diff`, `impact`, `suspect`, `pr-report` (preview) | not in Sphinx-Needs itself; ubCode, a separate useblocks product, documents diff and impact analysis[^ubcode] | diff and changelog between document versions, marked experimental by the project[^sd-features] | suspect-link detection: each item stores a `reviewed` fingerprint over its text, ref and link UIDs, and unreviewed changes are reported[^ds-item] | finds orphaned items and reports transitive defects; version-to-version diff *not verified*[^oft-readme] |
| **Interchange** | JSON, CSV, Markdown; SARIF, JUnit, ReqIF 1.2, JSON-LD (preview); read-only OSLC RM (experimental) | `needs.json` and per-need JSON; no ReqIF or JSON-LD export is documented in the builders reference[^sn-builders] | HTML, RST, JSON, Markdown, Excel, SPDX, Doxygen, ReqIF and HTML-to-PDF; ReqIF is marked experimental[^sd-formats][^sd-features] | publishes plain text, HTML, LaTeX and Markdown; exports and re-imports YAML, CSV, TSV and XLSX[^ds-publish][^ds-interchange] | reports in plain text, HTML and `aspec` XML; converts to `specobject` XML[^oft-guide] |
| **Editor support** | language server over stdio (preview); VS Code client (experimental) | the sphinx-needs-vscode extension is deprecated and unmaintained[^sn-vscode]; its replacement, ubCode, is free for public projects and requires a commercial licence otherwise[^ubcode-licence] | *none* — an LSP appears in the project's own backlog document, not in its features[^sd-backlog] | *not verified* | official JetBrains plugin; no LSP[^oft-guide] |
| **Ecosystem** | first release 2026-09-09, repository created 2026-08-26, 0 stars, 2 contributors, MIT[^stats] | since 2016, 301 stars, 58 contributors, MIT[^stats] | since 2020, 381 stars, 44 contributors, Apache-2.0[^stats] | since 2013, 660 stars, 52 contributors, LGPL-3.0[^stats] | since 2015, 167 stars, 22 contributors, GPL-3.0[^stats] |

### What the table does not show in Quarto-Needs' favour

Three things are worth saying outright, because a table invites reading
differences as advantages.

**The trace/effective distinction is not new.** OpenFastTrace has separated
shallow from deep coverage for years, and reports transitive defects when a
covering item is not itself covered.[^oft-guide] Quarto-Needs expresses the
same idea as a configurable percentage gate rather than a verdict; that is a
difference in form, not a capability the others lack.

**Suspect-link detection is not new either.** Doorstop fingerprints each
item's text, references and links, and reports unreviewed changes against
the recorded fingerprint.[^ds-item] That is the same job `suspect` does.

**The Sphinx-Needs ecosystem is larger than the Sphinx-Needs extension.**
Diff, impact analysis, source-code tracing and an editor integration all
exist for it through ubCode and sphinx-codelinks. ubCode is free for public
projects but needs a commercial licence for non-public ones,[^ubcode-licence]
which is a real difference for a closed-source team — but "Sphinx-Needs
cannot do impact analysis" would be false.

## Quarto-Needs' own surface, by tier {#surface}

Generated from the stability registry, so this cannot drift from what the
tool actually promises:

- **Stable**: `scan`, `check`, `coverage`, `trace`, `export`, `quality`, `query`, `baseline`, `baseline create`, `baseline inspect`, `diff`, `impact`, `export --format json|csv|markdown`, Quarto pre-render, Documented non-C4 shortcodes.

- **Preview**: `evidence`, `evidence check`, `suspect --git BASE..HEAD`, `pr-report --git BASE..HEAD`, `github-report --git BASE..HEAD`, `diff --git BASE..HEAD`, `impact --git BASE..HEAD`, `evidence attest`, `lsp`, `export --format sarif|junit|reqif|jsonld`.

- **Experimental**: `variant list|show NAME`, `migrate SOURCE`, `oslc discover|catalog|query|write`, C4 projections, GitHub Issues adapter, VS Code client.

## When not to use Quarto-Needs {#when-not}

**If you need a qualified tool, or anyone liable for it.** Quarto-Needs is
pre-1.0, has a single maintainer, carries no tool-qualification evidence,
and comes with no support contract. Parts of the feature set — evidence
with provenance, risk mitigation gates, ReqIF interchange — look like they
are aimed at regulated development. For the part of that audience that
needs a qualified tool, this project is disqualified, and no amount of test
coverage changes that. DOORS, Polarion and Codebeamer exist for this, and
so do the qualification packages sold with them.

**If you already live in the Sphinx ecosystem, use Sphinx-Needs.**
Quarto-Needs offers no Sphinx-Needs compatibility: not the directives, not
`needs.json`, not the configuration. Migrating means rewriting your
authoring layer for an incremental benefit, against a tool that has been
maintained since 2016 by 58 contributors. Sphinx-Needs is also better
supplied around the edges — schema validation on fields, constraints, and a
large body of existing projects to copy patterns from. Migration adapters in
this repository read the Sphinx-Needs export format; that is not a reason to
migrate, it is a way out if you have already decided to.

**If you want minimal traceability in a small repository, use Doorstop.**
It is simpler, older, more widely used, and its model — one YAML file per
item, a tree of documents, a validate command — is most of what a small
project needs. Quarto-Needs asks you to adopt Quarto and a typed graph
model; if you do not already want the document, that is overhead for a
result Doorstop gives you with less.

**If your requirements live next to code in many languages, use
OpenFastTrace.** Its tag importer recognises specification tags across a
long list of programming languages,[^oft-formats] and its shallow/deep
coverage model is mature. Quarto-Needs traces to components you declare in
the document, not to tags scattered across a polyglot source tree.

**If you want a GUI for non-programmer stakeholders, use StrictDoc.** It
ships an editable web interface that writes back to the underlying text
files.[^sd-map] Quarto-Needs has no editing UI and no plan for one; authors
edit `.qmd` files in an editor.

**The ecosystem gap is not closing on merit.** Zero stars and two
contributors against 167–660 stars and 22–58 contributors is a difference in
the number of people who will have hit your bug before you do, answered a
question you are about to ask, or fixed something you depend on. Technical
argument does not substitute for that, and choosing a tool with nobody else
using it is a real cost that should be counted.
